setupSteps: Warm up first. 2 to 3 minutes of gentle movement (ankle circles, a few bodyweight squats, cat-cows, hip circles). Never go deep cold.
Floor. Flat mat or carpet; avoid slippery tiles (feet can slide out).

Heel support. If the heels lift or you cannot reach low, place a folded or rolled blanket or towel under the heels (Yoga Journal; Yoga U Online; snippets). Keep the arches lifted; do not force the heels down.

Hip support (optional). Place a block, cushion or low stool 15 to 25 cm high (est.) between the feet to sit on if the hips will not reach the floor. Beginners can also stay at a half squat, hands on a chair seat.
Stance. Feet a little wider than the hips, toes turned out about 45 degrees (Yoga Journal; snippet); knees will track over the toes.
Hands. Hands in prayer at the chest, elbows ready to press into the inner knees; or hold a wall, door frame or chair for balance.
Clothing. Stretchy pants and a fitted top so the camera sees hips, knees and ankles; no tight jeans (they restrict the squat).

Camera. Phone at about hip height on a stool or shelf (about 60 to 90 cm, est.), about 2 m to the side, so the whole body from head to feet is in frame (see sections 11 and 12). A second front view checks the knees.

steps.title: Set the feet
steps.action: stand at the front of the mat, feet a little wider than the hips, toes turned out about 45 degrees.

steps.title: Place the heel support (if needed)
steps.action: slide a rolled blanket under both heels, or keep the heels flat on the mat.

steps.title: Start lowering
steps.action: bend the knees and send the hips back and down slowly, hands on a chair or wall if you want.
steps.feel: thighs working, a light stretch at the ankles and groin.

steps.title: Settle the hips
steps.action: lower as far as you can while the heels stay down and the back stays long; sit on a block if the hips do not reach the floor.
steps.feel: weight in the feet and the sitting bones, not the toes.

steps.title: Bring the palms together
steps.action: press the palms together at the chest, thumbs lightly touching the breastbone.
steps.feel: chest open, shoulders away from the ears.
steps.breathing: breathe in as the hands come together.

steps.title: Press elbows against the knees
steps.action: set the elbows on the inner knees and press them gently apart while the knees press back.
steps.feel: a gentle opening in the inner thighs and hips, with the knees tracking over the toes.

steps.title: Lengthen the spine
steps.action: lift the chest and the crown of the head, then grow tall on each in-breath.
steps.feel: the ribs lifting away from the hips; the tailbone heavy.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: stay with slow nose breaths. Beginners hold 5 breaths (about 30 seconds, est.); sources range from 10 to 30 seconds for the first tries up to 30 to 60 seconds, or 5 to 10 breaths.
steps.feel: a slow release in the groin and hips; weight even through both feet; no pain in the knees.
steps.breathing: slow nose breaths; never hold the breath.

steps.title: Rise slowly
steps.action: place the hands on the floor or a chair, press through the feet and stand up on an out-breath, with the chest lifted and the head last.

steps.title: Rest and repeat
steps.action: stand, shake out the legs and shift the weight side to side, then do a second round.

commonMistakes.title: Heels lifting off the floor
commonMistakes.text: Heels lifting off the floor. It points to tight calves or ankles (Yoga International: the deep calf muscle, the soleus, stays long when the knee is bent). Fix: roll a blanket under the heels, work on ankle mobility, and do not force them down.

commonMistakes.title: Rounding the spine (tucking the tailbone)
commonMistakes.text: Rounding the spine (tucking the tailbone). It compresses the back and limits depth. Fix: lift the chest, sit on a block, or squat less deeply.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving inward
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving inward. It stresses the inner knee and can come from weak glutes or tight inner thighs (Yoga International, snippet). Fix: press the elbows against the inner knees, turn the toes out a little more, and squat less deep.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the hips fast or bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the hips fast or bouncing. It loads the knees. Fix: lower in 4 to 5 seconds and rise slowly.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. It raises effort and blood pressure. Fix: slow nose breaths; count out-breaths.

commonMistakes.title: Forcing depth with knee or ankle pain
commonMistakes.text: Forcing depth with knee or ankle pain. Harvard Health advises avoiding deep squats if they hurt and keeping a small stool to sit on (snippet). Fix: use a block, a chair or a half squat; stop at pain.

commonMistakes.title: Gripping with the toes or rolling to the outer edges of the feet
commonMistakes.text: Gripping with the toes or rolling to the outer edges of the feet. It strains the arches and ankles. Fix: spread the toes and keep weight even across the feet.

commonMistakes.title: Rising too fast
commonMistakes.text: Rising too fast. Blood pressure can drop and cause dizziness (a standing yoga guide, snippet, warns sudden movements may cause dizziness or fainting). Fix: rise slowly with a hand on a chair or wall.

commonMistakes.title: Squatting on a full stomach or on slippery tiles
commonMistakes.text: Squatting on a full stomach or on slippery tiles. Fix: practise on a light or empty stomach and on a mat.

commonMistakes.title: Squatting for a long time every day
commonMistakes.text: Squatting for a long time every day. The strongest concern in the research is prolonged job-related kneeling or squatting (a 2000 case-control study linked it to knee osteoarthritis, with the highest risk in people with obesity; observational). Fix: hold a short time, rest between rounds, and stop at knee pain.

safetyNotes: Mild stretch, never pain. A gentle opening in the groin and hips and a light stretch at the ankles is normal; sharp pain, a pinch in the knee or hip, or tingling is not.

Knees and ankles: sources say to avoid the pose with knee, ankle, hip or groin injury or recent knee surgery (snippets). Harvard Health advises avoiding deep squats if they hurt. Use heel support, a block or a chair, and stop at knee pain.

Back: sources conflict on lower back pain (one says to avoid with knee or lower back pain; another says do not rely on it for back relief). Keep the spine long; a rounded, tucking back is the warning sign. Ask a doctor with a disc or spine problem.

Pregnancy: Mother.ly (snippet) describes a gentle squat that opens the pelvis and advises checking with a doctor or midwife first. Lamaze (snippet) advises against deep squats if the baby is engaged or in a posterior position. Ask a doctor or midwife; if cleared, a supported, shallow squat only.

Postpartum and after surgery: one yoga site lists postpartum, tearing or caesarean, spine surgery and hip replacement as reasons to avoid the pose (snippets). A fixed wait after birth or surgery: Not found; sources agree on provider clearance first.

Osteoporosis: a Mayo Clinic-linked case series (PubMed 22448849; snippet) raised concern about spinal flexion positions in osteopenia and osteoporosis; Osteoporosis Canada and other sources caution against deep hip openers and forward bends (snippets). The Malasana-specific verdict: Not found. Ask a doctor; if cleared, keep the spine long, avoid rounding, and use a chair.

Blood pressure and heart: a 2013 study found blood pressure rises during yoga, most in standing poses; breath-holding is not recommended with hypertension (snippets). Malasana is not named in these sources. Move slowly, never hold the breath, and rise slowly to avoid dizziness.
Stop immediately if you feel: sharp knee, hip or ankle pain, numbness or tingling, dizziness or faintness, chest pain or breathlessness, back pain, or pelvic, abdominal or incision pain.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: keep the mat out of walkways; do not hog the stretching area.

Naming: several sources use Malasana for different squats (foot width, prayer hands). We present the garland pose and do not claim it is a Common Yoga Protocol posture.
Hold time: 10 seconds up to 30 to 60 seconds, or 5 to 10 breaths. We chose 5 slow breaths (about 30 s, est.), no breath-holding.

Squatting and knees: prolonged job-related squatting linked to knee osteoarthritis versus reviews calling moderate deep squatting beneficial or fears unfounded. We chose "short holds, pain is the guide, modify with knee pain".

Pregnancy: gentle supported squat (Mother.ly, Lamaze) versus avoiding it if the baby is engaged or posterior and pelvic floor strain from intense squatting. We chose "ask a doctor; supported shallow only if cleared".
Lower back pain: one source says avoid with back pain; another says do not rely on it for back relief. We chose "modify; ask a doctor with a disc problem or ongoing pain".

Not found: Ministry of AYUSH Common Yoga Protocol, MDNIY and The Yoga Institute (Mumbai) pages for Malasana; a pose-specific MET; measured joint-angle norms for the held pose; trial evidence for this pose alone; a fixed wait after birth or surgery; clinical sources for cholesterol, thyroid, heart disease and surgery for this pose. Our thresholds are estimates.
Most pages were seen only as search snippets or summaries; direct page fetches were not possible.
